Impunity
ĭm-pū´nĭ-ty
n. (exemption from punishment or the consequences of an act)
Latin impunitas, from in, not, and poena, punishment. The word names what the wicked appear to enjoy and what Scripture says they do not have.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Impunity is escape from punishment, and Scripture denies it twice over. Of the wicked: “though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished” (Pro 11:21; 16:5). Of the delay that produces the appearance of it: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecc 8:11). Of the certainty: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7). And the Name itself closes the door: the LORD is merciful and gracious, “and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines impunity as exemption from punishment or penalty; freedom from injury, loss, or harm.

expand to see more

IMPUNITY, n. Exemption from punishment or penalty.

2. Freedom or exemption from injury.

3. Exemption from loss or other ill consequence.

Key Scripture

Pro 11:21 — "Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered."

Ecc 8:11 — "Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil."

Gal 6:7 — "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap."

Exo 34:7 — "Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation."

Num 32:23 — "But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out."

Modern Corruption

Delay is read as acquittal, and Ecclesiastes says the delay is exactly why men's hearts are set to do evil.

expand to see more

Ecclesiastes 8:11 is the most precise sentence in Scripture on how impunity is manufactured. Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. The mechanism is not that men conclude there is no judgment; it is that the interval erodes the sense of one, and the conclusion is reached by the body before the mind states it. Every sin a man commits repeatedly he first got away with once, and the getting away with it did the persuading.

Numbers 32:23 is the plainest denial: be sure your sin will find you out — and the grammar is worth noting, because the sin is the subject and the finding is its own act. It is not that someone will find out about the sin; the sin will find the sinner. Galatians 6:7 says the same in the language of agriculture, and adds the reason the delay does not help: sowing and reaping are separated by a season in every field, and no farmer takes the interval as evidence that the seed has died.

The doctrine is not a threat held over Christians, and the same Bible that denies impunity gives the ground on which the guilty go free. Exodus 34:7 says God will by no means clear the guilty, and Romans 3:26 says how He is nevertheless the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus: the penalty was not waived but borne. What the gospel offers is not impunity but substitution, and the difference is the whole of Christianity. A man who thinks he has been let off has not understood what happened; he has been paid for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naqah (H5352), to be clean, go unpunished; lo yinnaqeh, shall not be unpunished; Greek mukterizo (G3456), to mock, turn up the nose at.

Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be unpunished, held innocent; Proverbs 11:21, 16:5, 28:20, Exodus 34:7, Jeremiah 25:29.

Greek mukterizo (G3456) — to mock; Galatians 6:7, God is not mocked.

Hebrew matsa (H4672) — to find; Numbers 32:23, your sin will find you out.

Usage

"“Sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily” — how impunity is manufactured."

"“Be sure your sin will find you out” — the sin is the subject of the sentence."

"“Will by no means clear the guilty” — and yet the justifier of him which believeth."
